Feeling or showing anger because something seems unfair, unjust, or disrespectful — especially something that wounds your sense of dignity or violates your sense of what is right.
Why it's different from ordinary anger

Not all anger is the same. You can be angry because you're hungry, because you lost a game, or because your phone died. That's general anger — it can come from anywhere.

But indignant anger is more specific. It always comes from a feeling that something wrong was done — that you were treated in a way you didn't deserve, that an unfair accusation was made against you, or that someone looked down on you when they had no right to. There's a strong sense of moral injury to it. You're not just upset — you feel that justice or basic decency has been violated.

Think of it this way: indignant = anger + a deep sense of "this is not right and I don't deserve this."
The feeling from the inside

When someone is indignant, they typically feel two things at once: anger and a sense of righteous self-belief — meaning they are firmly convinced they are in the right. An indignant person isn't confused or guilty. They're sure. That certainty is part of what makes the feeling so sharp and charged.

It also carries a wounded quality. Something about your dignity, your reputation, or your sense of fairness has been hurt. That's why the word shares a root with "dignity" and "indignity."
What triggers it

You feel indignant when:

You are falsely accused of something. You are insulted or belittled. You are dismissed or not taken seriously when you deserve to be. Someone breaks a rule or acts in a way you find morally wrong. You are treated as less than you are.
What an indignant person looks, sounds, and acts like

An indignant person might raise their voice, go cold and stiff, refuse to back down, or speak in a very sharp, clipped tone. They might say things like "How dare you!" or "That is completely unfair!" or "I can't believe you would suggest that." Their body language often shows it too — crossed arms, a sharp stare, a raised chin. The overall impression is someone who feels their dignity has been challenged and is pushing back.
Using it in sentences

She was indignant when her teacher accused her of cheating on a test she had studied hard for.

He shot an indignant look at the man who cut in front of him in the queue.

"I have never been so insulted in my life," she said, her voice indignant.

The workers were indignant that their pay had been cut without any explanation.
Can you be indignant on someone else's behalf?

Yes, absolutely. You don't have to be the person who was wronged. If you witness someone being treated unfairly — a stranger being publicly humiliated, a friend being blamed for something they didn't do — you can feel indignant for them. The trigger is still the same: a perceived injustice. It just happens to someone else instead of you.
When "indignant" carries a slightly critical tone

This is an important nuance. Sometimes, describing someone as indignant is a subtle way of suggesting their anger is excessive or self-righteous — that they're making too big a deal of something minor, or that they think too highly of themselves. If someone gets indignant because a restaurant brought them the wrong type of bread, the word "indignant" in that context quietly signals that their reaction is overblown. So the word is accurate and neutral when the outrage is justified, but it can carry a faintly mocking or critical flavor when the situation doesn't really warrant such strong feelings.
The difference between similar words

Angry is the broad, general term — any kind of anger for any reason.

Indignant is a type of anger specifically tied to a perceived injustice or insult to one's dignity.

Outraged is stronger and louder — it's indignation turned up to a high volume, often over something more serious or public.

Offended is softer — it means your feelings were hurt, but it doesn't carry the same sense of righteous fire that indignant does.
Related word forms you'll encounter

Indignantly (adverb) — describes how someone does something. "She indignantly denied the accusation."

Indignation (noun) — the feeling or state itself. "He could barely contain his indignation."

Indignity (noun) — an event or treatment that is insulting or humiliating. "He suffered the indignity of being fired in front of his colleagues."
The one-sentence summary
Indignant means feeling a specific kind of sharp, righteous anger — the kind that arises when you believe something deeply unfair or disrespectful has been done to you or to someone else.
